posts.image_headline: THE DITCH THAT BUILT NEW YORK
posts.caption:
🛶 ON THIS DAY in 1825, a governor set off from Lake Erie for New York with two barrels of lake water. What he did with them made history.

On 26 October 1825, the Erie Canal opened. Governor DeWitt Clinton boarded the packet boat Seneca Chief at Buffalo and headed east.

Critics had mocked the project as "Clinton's Big Ditch". It ran 363 miles from Lake Erie to the Hudson River at Albany, climbed 568 feet through 83 locks, and cost about $7 million after eight years of work.

Eight days later, at New York, Clinton poured the Lake Erie water into the Atlantic. People called it the "marriage of the waters".

The ditch paid off. Shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York fell from about $100 by road to $10 by canal. Within 15 years, New York was the busiest port in the United States.

Would you have backed Clinton's "Big Ditch", or joined the people laughing at it?

posts.topic: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the Great Pyramid
posts.title: Cleopatra is closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramids
posts.hook_text: CLEOPATRA IS CLOSER TO US THAN PYRAMIDS

scenes.narration: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramids.
scenes.label: TIME IS WILD

scenes.narration: The Great Pyramid was built for the pharaoh Khufu, about 4,500 years ago.
scenes.label: c. 2560 BC

scenes.narration: Cleopatra was born around 69 BC. By then, that pyramid was already about 2,500 years old.
scenes.label: 2,500 YEARS

scenes.narration: From her birth to Apollo 11 landing on the Moon is only about 2,000 years.
She wasn't even from an Egyptian family. She descended from Ptolemy, a Macedonian Greek general of Alexander the Great.
scenes.label: PTOLEMY I

scenes.narration: Her dynasty ruled Egypt for about three centuries. She is the only one of them known to have learned Egyptian.
scenes.label: 300 YEARS

scenes.narration: To Cleopatra, the pyramids were already ancient monuments. After her death in 30 BC, Egypt became a Roman province.
scenes.label: 30 BC

scenes.narration: Which history fact messes with your sense of time? Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🏺 HISTORY'S WEIRDEST: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

The pyramid was about 2,500 years old when she was born. From her birth to Apollo 11 is about 2,000 years.

Which history fact messes with your sense of time?

🏜️ HE FAKED A VOW TO SEE A LOST CITY. In 1812, a Swiss traveller risked his life for one look at a place no European had seen in centuries.

Johann Ludwig Burckhardt had studied Arabic and Islamic law so he could pass as a Muslim. He travelled as "Sheikh Ibrahim Ibn Abdallah".

In what is now Jordan, he heard of ruins hidden in a valley. Asking openly could expose him. So he said he had vowed to sacrifice a goat at the tomb of Aaron, Moses's brother, which lay beyond them.

On 22 August 1812, his guide led him in. He saw rock-cut tombs, the facade now called the Treasury, a theatre and a temple.

He was convinced this was Petra, the capital of the Nabataeans, a people who grew rich on desert trade routes. But his guides grew suspicious, and he had to cut the visit short.

He was 27. Five years later he fell ill and died in Cairo, aged 32.

Would you have risked the disguise for one look?

posts.topic: The Mary Rose, Henry VIII's sunken warship
posts.image_headline: THE KING WATCHED HIS WARSHIP SINK
posts.caption:
⚓ LOST & FOUND: Henry VIII watched his great warship sink in minutes. 437 years later, 60 million people watched it come back up.

On 19 July 1545, the Mary Rose sailed out against a French fleet in the Solent, off Portsmouth. The king was watching from Southsea Castle.

As she turned, she heeled over, water rushed in through her open gunports, and she went down. Of roughly 500 men aboard, only about 30 to 35 survived.

Why? No one knows for sure. A Flemish survivor blamed a sudden gust of wind. Others point to it being the captain's first naval command, or to heavy new guns.

Divers found the wreck again in 1971. On 11 October 1982, after more than 27,000 dives, her hull was lifted from the seabed live on television.

Around 19,000 objects have been recovered, including 82 nit combs: a rare look at daily life on a Tudor warship.

What would you most want to see from the wreck?

posts.topic: Breaking the Enigma code, from Warsaw to Bletchley Park
posts.title: The Unbreakable Machine: How the Enigma Code Was Really Cracked

scenes.narration: In May 1941, British sailors climbed into a crippled German U-boat in the North Atlantic. Inside was a prize worth more than the submarine: an Enigma machine and its codebooks.
scenes.label: 9 MAY 1941

scenes.narration: The U-boat was allowed to sink the next day, and everyone involved was sworn to secrecy. Germany believed its cipher machine could not be broken.
This is how Polish mathematicians, then thousands of people at an English country house, cracked that machine, the one flaw that helped them, and the secret they kept for decades.
Enigma looked like a typewriter in a wooden box. Press a key, and electric current ran through a set of rotors, lighting up a different letter.
After every key press, a rotor turned, so the same letter came out differently each time. A plugboard at the front swapped pairs of letters again.
After changes in 1939, the army and air force machines could be set up in about fifteen billion billion ways. And the settings changed every day.
scenes.label: 1.5×10^19 WAYS

scenes.narration: German forces used Enigma on land, at sea and in the air. Anyone who could read it could see their orders.
The first people to break Enigma were not British. In September 1932, a 27-year-old Polish mathematician, Marian Rejewski, began his attack on it.
scenes.label: SEPT 1932

scenes.narration: He worked for the Polish Cipher Bureau with two fellow mathematicians, Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski.
French intelligence passed the Poles German manuals for the machine. Rejewski wrote equations to model its scrambling, and by the end of 1932 he had worked out the wiring of the military rotors.
scenes.label: END OF 1932

scenes.narration: Polish engineers built working copies of Enigma. The team invented the clock method, perforated Zygalski sheets, and a machine called the bomba to hunt for the settings.
Then, in December 1938, Germany added two new rotors. Instead of six possible rotor orders, there were now sixty. Poland could not afford the extra machines.
In July 1939, just outside Warsaw, the Poles shared everything with British and French codebreakers, including copies of Enigma. Five weeks later, Germany invaded Poland.
scenes.label: JULY 1939

scenes.narration: The British codebreakers worked at Bletchley Park, a mansion in Buckinghamshire known as Station X. When the war began, around 200 people worked there.
scenes.label: STATION X

scenes.narration: Among them was a young mathematician, Alan Turing. Building on the Polish bomba, he designed a far more powerful machine: the bombe.
Gordon Welchman added a clever refinement called the diagonal board. The first bombe, named Victory, was installed on 18 March 1940.
scenes.label: 18 MAR 1940

scenes.narration: Each bombe weighed about a ton. It tested rotor positions against a crib: a guessed piece of text that probably appeared in the message.
scenes.label: 1 TON

scenes.narration: One flaw helped enormously. Enigma never turned a letter into itself. That alone let codebreakers rule out impossible guesses.
By the end of the war, around 200 bombes had been built in Britain and America. Wrens of the Women's Royal Naval Service ran many of them around the clock.
scenes.label: ~200 BOMBES

scenes.narration: Naval Enigma was among the hardest to crack. That is why U-110 mattered so much: it handed Britain a machine with its rotors set, and the current codebooks.
scenes.label: U-110

scenes.narration: It is almost certain that the material helped the Allies sink many U-boats. To protect the secret, the U-110 survivors were interned and never knew their boat had been captured.
By late 1944, nearly 9,000 people worked at Bletchley in three shifts around the clock. About three quarters of them were women.
scenes.label: 9,000 STAFF

scenes.narration: In January 1944 came Colossus, an early electronic computer with 1,600 vacuum tubes, built to attack a different German cipher machine.
When the war ended, the codebreakers stayed silent. The work remained secret until 1974, when Frederick Winterbotham was allowed to publish The Ultra Secret.
Experts suggest the codebreakers may have shortened the war by as much as two years. Yet Bletchley staff received no official honours until 2009.
scenes.label: 2 YEARS?

scenes.narration: Marian Rejewski, the man who first broke Enigma, survived the war and lived until 1980.
Who deserves the most credit for cracking Enigma: the Polish pioneers, Turing's team at Bletchley, or the sailors who boarded U-110? Tell us in the comments.

posts.caption:
🔐 THE UNBREAKABLE CODE: Germany believed Enigma was unbreakable. Polish mathematicians broke it first, in 1932.

Then came Bletchley Park, Alan Turing's bombes, a captured U-boat, and a secret kept until 1974.

Who deserves the most credit for cracking Enigma?

posts.topic: The Lady Be Good, the B-24 bomber found in the Libyan desert
posts.title: The bomber found in the Sahara 16 years after it vanished
posts.hook_text: THIS BOMBER VANISHED. FOUND 16 YEARS LATER.

scenes.narration: Oil explorers flying over Libya's desert spotted a bomber lost since 1943.
She was the Lady Be Good, a B-24 on her crew's first combat mission: a raid on Naples.
scenes.label: 4 APR 1943

scenes.narration: Flying home in the dark, the pilot reported a faulty direction finder. They flew right past their base.
scenes.label: SOLUCH

scenes.narration: They probably thought they were still over the sea. When the fuel ran out, all nine men bailed out into the night.
scenes.label: 9 MEN

scenes.narration: With half a canteen of water between them, eight walked north. Five covered about 78 miles. One went 109.
scenes.label: 109 MILES

scenes.narration: They lasted eight days. The co-pilot's diary was found in his pocket: "Still waiting for help, still praying."
scenes.label: 8 DAYS

scenes.narration: When a team reached the wreck in 1959, its radio still worked. The ninth man has never been found.
Would you have stayed with the plane, or walked? Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
✈️ UNSOLVED FILES: In 1958, oil explorers spotted a US bomber in the Libyan desert. It had been missing since April 1943.

Its nine crewmen had bailed out, lost and out of fuel, hundreds of miles inland. One of them walked 109 miles. One has never been found.

Would you have stayed with the plane, or walked?
